speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask leave of the House to present a motion under Standing Order 43. Usually, when one presents such a request under Standing Order 43, it is assumed that one is asking for the entire House to agree to the substance of the proposition. In this case I know that the substance of what I am asking for has not yet been agreed to; therefore I am simply asking for what is provided in Standing Order 43, namely, that consent be given to the making of the motion so the House can decide whether it agrees with the substance of the proposition.
Therefore, in view of the $75 million welfare budget in the city of Toronto and similar high costs in other cities and in other parts of the country I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather):
That this House urges the government to give immediate consideration to the raising of the federal share of costs under the Canada Assistance Plan from 50 per cent to 65 per cent during any fiscal year in which unemployment in Canada exceeds 3 per cent of the labour force.

MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the imminent takeover and foreign control of Home Oil Company of Calgary by Ashland Oil Incorporated of Kentucky, and the vital necessity for Parliament to consider ways and means of preventing the last major Canadian-owned and controlled oil company from being sold to non-residents, this subject being of equal importance to the Prime Minister's interruption of an emergency debate on March 2, 1971, to announce that the government would prevent the sale of control in Denison Mines Limited to non-residents.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has given the notice required under Standing Order 26, and I have considered the matter most attentively. The matter raised by the hon. member

February 9, 1971
The Canadian Economy
is one which is of national interest and concern to all members of the House. This has been indicated by the number of questions which have been asked on a number of days during the last week or so. Indeed, it seems to me that this is the very kind of situation which appears to be contemplated by Standing Order 26. In ordinary circumstances, the motion could very well have been put to the House.
The spirit of the Standing Order is that hon. members should be given an opportunity to discuss an urgent matter of national importance within a reasonable time. However, it has already been indicated to the House that tomorrow and Thursday would be set aside for the consideration of the budget debate. These will be the last two days spent on that debate. These two days will provide an opportunity to consider the problem raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands.
I had some reservations about this possibility at first, thinking that a number of hon. members had already taken part in the budget debate. But since only two hon. members spoke on the main motion-the others spoke on the amendment and subamendment-just about every hon. member except two will have an opportunity, if they want to and provided the necessary time is available, to participate in the debate. If I may make a suggestion, which may be beyond my competence and jurisdiction, an arrangement might be made among the House Leaders regarding the setting of a time limitation of the speeches which can be made during the next two days. In other words, I suggest to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that it would be very difficult for the Chair on the eve of a general debate to say that we should have a special debate under the terms of Standing Order 26.
Again I insist that I recognize that this is the kind of matter which might very well be the subject of a debate under the provisions of Standing Order 26, but because there has already been an indication that tomorrow and the day after will be provided for the study of problems such as this one I do not think I could allow the hon. member's motion at this time.

Mr. Speaker, on February 2, as recorded on page 2976 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources "whether the government is prepared to exercise the same powers with respect to Home Oil Company remaining in Canadian hands as were exercised by the government with respect to Denison Mines." The minister replied at that time:
I cannot speak for the government in that regard at this time. That would be a matter for the government to decide.

As the hon. member knows, in the case of Denison the federal authority had declared that uranium was a work for the general advantage of Canada. In that case there was no problem with respect to constitutional authority. I do not think the situation is quite as clear with respect to oil.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Acting Prime Minister if I am to take from his remarks that the government considers that the retention in Canadian hands of a share in the oil industry, which in the foreseeable future will probably be the largest industry in Canada, is not just as important as keeping control of part of the uranium industry in Canadian hands?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman knows, I think there might be some resistance on the part of the provinces if the federal Parliament were to take complete jurisdiction over oil. That, it seems to me, is the difference between the uranium case, in which many years ago a declaration was made that uranium is a work for the general advantage of Canada, and the kind of situation that now exists in the oil industry.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, February 4, consideration in committee of Bill C-207, respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto-Mr. Trudeau-Mr. Honey in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Thursday, February 4, clause 5 of the bill was under consideration. Shall clause 5 carry?
On clause 5-Duties of minister.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with clause 5 of Part I of Bill C-207. I do not think we spent too much time discussing this clause last Thursday, and there are several points which I would like to make today. I would point out to hon. members that the clause as presently constituted gives the new minister a rather limited function so far as the total environmental picture is concerned. During second reading, a number of members of the parties on this side of the House expressed a desire that the minister's duties be expanded to cover all problems relating to pollution and pollution prevention. I again want to stress the need for an overall authority so far as pollution is concerned.
Surely, Canadians have learned from past experience that the division of jurisdiction for pollution among a number of departments has just not worked. It is the reason we are faced with major pollution problems from one end of the country to the other. We must have some minister in a position to oversee all pollution problems, in a position to set national standards and to see that they are enforced. One minister must be responsible for co-ordination and co-operation between the various departments with regard to environmental problems.
Government Organization Act, 1970 Until we get that type of organization, we will not effectively reach the root of the problems.
I notice that several major areas which have pollution problems are excluded from the provisions of clause 5, and omitted from the jurisdiction of the new department. Again, I point to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, which comprise 40 per cent of Canada's total area. The ecology of that area is extremely fragile. It is an area which should be directly under the control of the new department of the environment, yet it is being excluded. This does not make sense in any way, shape or form. The department must have authority to move into the north and do a proper job of pollution prevention.
At present we have no land use regulations for the Northwest Territories. They are in the process of being drafted, but over a period of years exploration has been taking place on an increasing scale in the north. Ecologists, and others who have done research, have told us that if we get a major oil spill or major pollution problem in some of the big Arctic rivers, Canada will be in real trouble. This immense, newly developing area should come under the control of the minister of the environment with regard to pollution matters.
A number of other areas are also omitted from the new department's control. Again, I stress it is absolutely essential to have one department act as a kind of umbrella over all other departments when dealing with the pollution problems of the nation. I have spoken on this matter previously, and I hope to ask questions of the minister once more. At the moment I would like to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West:
That clause 5 of Bill C-207 be amended by striking out the first seven lines of the section and substituting the following:
The duties, powers and functions of the Minister of the Environment extend to and include all matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to pollution prevention and control and to

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: If the hon. member has concluded his remarks, I will put the amendment.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Before I sit down may I just say a word or two about the amendment. If adopted, it would do the job that I have suggested should be done. It would give the new department control over all pollution problems. It is a good amendment. It is what we have been fighting for over a number of years, and I think the committee should accept it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the Committee ready for the question? Shall the said amendment carry?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the face of it this amendment purports to be both a simplification and expansion of the phraseology contained in the bill The difference between the wording of the amendment and the wording of the bill is the removal of the clarifying phrase, "not by law assigned to any other department, branch or agency of the Government of Canada." I think this clarifying phrase is important. This is in the nature of a residual clause, that all the jurisdiction related to pollution problems is vested in the minister except where Parliament,

February 9, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 in relation to a particular matter, has expressly decreed otherwise.
To accept the amendment would, in effect, be acting in a manner contrary to the expressed intention of Parliament in either past instances or in future cases, and I do not think the House would really want to do this. I think hon. members feel the House should be free to assign specific duties to particular departments in the legislation covering their particular jurisdictions, even though to some degree they relate to pollution, or pollution prevention and control, rather than vest the supreme, the overriding authority in this particular minister.
The intention, obviously, of the current bill is this: where pollution is the primary concern of Parliament, unless it is decreed that that particular matter shall be under the jurisdiction of some other department, it shall be under the jurisdiction of the new minister of the environment. I think that this is the type of provision which allows the House full freedom to make specific exemptions from the general control where, in its view, it is necessary. For that reason, the government would not wish to support this amendment.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board. I speak in support of the amendment, because it seems to me that one of the problems we face as Canadians is fighting this sinister force known as pollution that can, if left unchecked, destroy us all. I was interested in the minister's remarks about Parliaments of the future. Many of us are concerned in case our future is rather limited. It will be unless we actively, positively and ruthlessly do something to solve this particular problem. The battle against pollution has not been conducted in a comprehensive way because responsibility for pollution control is split among many levels of government, federal, provincial and, of course, municipal. Also, the responsibility is split among so many ministries at the federal and provincial level that the prosecution of offences and the correction of excesses is exceedingly difficult.
Some of us who are interested in this matter had hoped that the government intended designating the minister of the new department as the person with supreme responsibility in our country for the fight against pollution. We hoped that he was to be the veritable czar in matters of pollution. The public, I think, is concerned about pollution control. If we are to heed the public's justifiable concern over pollution, it seems to me that we ought to invest the minister with the power he needs to combat pollution at every level. Is the idea of a czar in the field of pollution control mere window dressing? If it is not window dressing, why cannot he be given the power he needs to combat pollution at all levels?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will speak briefly. I support the amendment wholeheartedly. In the past, the government has displayed a wishy-washy attitude towards pollution. Pollution has taken the place of motherhood; everybody is for it, so long as no one has to do
too much about it. That has been the attitude of the government, as illustrated by the Canada water bill.
I think the problem we face has been set out precisely by the hon. member who moved the amendment. Jurisdiction in the field is divided. I know the President of the Treasury Board has said that Parliament has decreed otherwise. I think Parliament has decreed otherwise wrongly. This amendment is an attempt to rectify the situation, and would also make sure that pollution could be dealt with as a single issue by a single minister. As a matter of fact, I think that pollution ought to be a matter of discussion today, at the federal-provincial conference.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Someone says that it is. How do we know that?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had expected to be asked to explain why the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry is not present today. The fact of the matter is that, right now, he is at the federal-provincial conference to discuss pollution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Of course, he is over there to discuss pollution. But is he urging the provincial governments to agree with the federal government that the direction of the battle against pollution which threatens all humanity and all citizens of our country should be placed under a single administration? The pollution problems that we shall have to face in this country for a long time are the problems that peoples of all countries will have to face. Nevertheless, we have seen the government adopting a very wishy-washy approach to the matter. It is fine for the minister to talk about pollution; everyone loves to hear talk of pollution control. But what is the government doing to control pollution? There is before the committee a sensible amendment. I support it wholeheartedly. I hope the mild words I have spoken will induce some government members to support it as well.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the President of the Treasury Board a question? Why has he specifically omitted the Northwest Territories and the Yukon area from the jurisdiction of the new minister?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although it seems to me that the government is determined to defeat the amendment, may I say this. It seems to me that the government will ignore the economic developments in the north and bypass the environmental problems of that area. I do not think there is any doubt about it, and the people of the area know this. For years, many environmental problems of that area have been ignored, and that is why there are no land use regulations today to control the current economic developments. It is true that those regulations may be introduced later. I submit that the failure to include one of the most vulnerable parts of our nation under this bill is a disaster.

If the government does not like my amendment, let it bring in some other appropriate amendment to cover the point I have been trying to make. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make two points. I find the minister's argument against this amendment very weak. I would like to express to him some sympathy since I feel he has been placed in a most difficult position this afternoon, inasmuch as the minister who will be responsible for the implementation of the various aspects of this part of the bill is not in the Chamber. This is unfortunate for the quality of the debate and for our attempt to determine the best legislation possible.
The minister has made a number of arguments, some of which have been dealt with. A moment ago he suggested that if this matter is important it should be referred to someone outside the House. It seems to me that that approach is contrary to the way this institution operates. On the other hand, if the minister is arguing that the proposition is already covered by the bill, then I cannot see what his argument is all about. He seemed to indicate in another argument that perhaps it was taken care of under clause 5(e). I feel there is something fundamental involved here, and it is to that that I direct the attention of the committee for a moment.
Five, 10 or 15 years ago, a debate on the establishment of this kind of department would have seemed irrelevant
[Mr. Drury.)
February 9, 1971

to the point of ridiculousness. It was not the thing then to be concerned about the future, or the possible non-future, of the environment. But in the last decade we have heard increasingly of the danger of pollution, so much so that now a great body of material has been written indicating that the natural resources of this earth are not inexhaustible, and certainly not those within our own jurisdiction.
There seems to be one attitude-perhaps this is the attitude reflected by what the government is about to do-that we should merely take some kind of band-aid approach to what is really a most basic problem. This approach to pollution is:	"We will simply try and
muddle through as best we can and dampen down the most glaring evidences of pollution that affect some aspect of our land, our water or our air". If the minister's attitude is being correctly reflected here this afternoon, there seems to be a willingness to adopt a kind of fire engine approach in which you rush in, put some water on the fire, and hope that everything will be taken care of, instead of having a positive desire to, in some instances, effect a very major restructuring of industries or undertakings that are continually contributing to pollution.
The minister indicated a few moments ago that it was very difficult to define what is meant by "controlling pollution". However, that is the phrase used in the bill. It may be that we are faced with some kind of good-guy approach and there will be an attempt to deal with the problems of pollution without causing too much sweat or getting too many people upset. That approach may satisfy some people but it certainly does not satisfy me, and I do not think it satisfies the hon. member who introduced this amendment.
I suggest that if we are serious about dealing with pollution, we must concern ourselves with preventive measures. We must, in many cases, get at the root cause of pollution, which in itself is a continuing problem. In the final analysis, if we are to make a major change in our attitude in this country, the emphasis will not be placed on controlling pollution, because that could mean anything. Certainly, it does not indicate the department is going to adopt the attitude of trying to eliminate pollution; it simply means that the department is going to involve itself in some way with pollution, which might amount merely to making some kind of report on a regular basis, or taking some other superficial or limited approach to the problem. If the commitment of this new department is, in effect, the eradication of pollution, then the word "prevention" must be in this bill. It is not just a question of semantics; it is a question of basic attitude.
If the minister feels, as he mentioned a moment ago, that there is an important question of interpretation and that there is a sophistication beyond this House in terms of drafting this legislation, then I suggest we should allow the clause to stand. I think this whole matter will have to be debated quite seriously at some stage, but in this instance at least if he feels there is a question which
Government Organization Act, 1970 should be resolved by the law officers of the Crown, or whoever drafted this bill in its final form, surely we should allow the clause to stand. I do not want to put words into the hon. member's mouth, but I am sure the mover of this amendment would be quite willing to allow it to stand so that there could be sufficient consultation to clear up any difficulties and make sure it will not jeopardize any other legal aspect of the bill.
I suggest it will not be enough for this government to say: "Sure, this is what we mean. We are concerned with the eradication of pollution, or, we are concerned primarily with preventing pollution and that is the reason we are setting up this new department". Words from the minister or any other members of this House, if I may say so without disrespect to their own worth or sincerity, mean nothing. They mean nothing in so far as the legal interpretation of this bill is concerned. If we are serious, and if the government is serious, in eliminating, removing and preventing pollution, then clear-cut language has to be used in the establishment of this new department. I do not really think it is possible for the minister to pass the matter off by saying it is a question of definition or the problem is already covered in some sort of general way.
The essence of the commitment of this government and this department is, in fact, to eradicate pollution from this country. This is about as basic as anything can be in respect of the establishment of this department and in respect of dealing effectively with the growing problems of pollution in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should try to find sin where it is not easily perceptible. There is nothing in the amendment that would in any way suggest the environmental council shall cause a charge to be levied on the Crown. It may well be that if the amendment were passed, the government would be faced with the responsibility of finding dedicated people, either within the public service or outside it, who would serve on this council. I think the Chair must find, as a condition precedent to saying that the amendment is not in order, that it actually contains a provision which would logically lead the Chair to believe that a charge will be made against the Crown. Putting it in reverse, without authority being granted in a statute, no funds can be provided in the estimates. This amendment does not purport to enable the government to pay anybody. As I said, the amendment may create some problems for the government in finding people who will serve on the council, but there is nothing in the amendment to suggest that money would have to be expended.
It is a dicey problem, comme ci comme ga. I suggest, however, that under these circumstances the Chair would be justified in accepting the amendment. There is a rule which provides that the Chair should be vigilant in trying to find an amendment is in order. However, unless an examination of the amendment reveals a clear direction which will result in a charge upon the Crown,- while we may be faced with some doubt as to what will be the result of the amendment-the amendment cannot be ruled out of order. It is not for the Chair to decide what the result of the amendment will be. The Chair must decide whether this amendment specifically provides for a charge. If it does not, I submit with great deference that it should be considered to be in order.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure that it is necessary to force upon you the necessity of making a ruling as to whether providing an option constitutes a charge on the crown or does not. I think it is well known that under a variety of general statutes the minister, subject to approval under the Appropriations Act, has the power to appoint advisers to himself. The basic purpose of this amendment is to provide for the setting up of a body to provide the minister with advice. The minister now has authority under other statutes to do this, as I say, subject to approval under the Appropriations Act. Therefore, it may be we are not giving him any authority he does not now enjoy, or will enjoy once the bill is passed. In any event, in either case, approval must he had under the Appropriations Act. I say that this general authority does exist and has been exercised in a number of cases.
I would ask-and perhaps the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry might reinforce this-whether it is wise at this point to specify in such detail the kind of body that should be set up to provide him with advice. I think it is probably more appropriate not to limit his freedom of action in this way, but rather to give him an opportunity, under the general authority that he has, to find from time to time the advisers he needs as he proceeds and as circumstances change. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, on the question of providing an option for the minister to set up an environmental council of Canada and whether or not such action involves additional expense, may I point out that the amendment as proposed does not impose any additional cost on the crown other than the cost that the crown itself may decide to impose and has the power to impose. If the crown were to decide not to set up an environmental council, then that would be the crown's decision, of course. If it decides it will set up an environmental council and provides funds for so doing, then again that is a decision that the crown is making; it is not being made by this House. Consequently, it seems to me that no additional cost would be imposed upon the Crown if this amendment were accepted.
With reference to the point raised by the President of the Treasury Board, I might agree with him as to the specific terms of reference. It might be wiser either not to include them or to couch them in more general terms, but I do not think it is sufficient merely to leave to the discretion of the minister whether to have advisers. It is
taken for granted that any minister will secure the advice of experts in his particular field. There should be set up an environmental council which would bring in not only experts but involve representatives of provincial governments, municipal bodies and the general public in one form or another in order to secure the participation of groups particularly concerned about pollution in Canada. It seems to me that this is a desirable step. All that this amendment is proposing is that the minister shall have the power to set up such a council if and when he deems it advisable to do so, and then only when he can persuade his colleagues to authorize the expenditure of money for that purpose.
If the President of the Treasury Board were prepared to accept an amendment that gives the minister the option of setting up an environmental council, if and when he is ready to do so and when his colleagues agree, then it might be possible to put the terms of reference in much more general form, or alternatively to omit any specifics except that the environmental council would embrace experts in the field and also encompass those organizations that have manifested their concern with regard to pollution of the environment.

This may very well be desirable but I do not think we should deal with it in a bill of this kind, certainly not in a bill that deals specifically with one minister.

The common practice under the English parliamentary system, and certainly in the cabinets with which I am familiar, is that each minister is responsible for his own department and for the administration of statutes which fall within the ambit of that department. Where a subject is all-embracing, such as finance, for example, or in this case environment, and several departments, ministers and powers are involved, the reconciliation of any differences has to be made by the government as a whole in the cabinet and under the direction of the Prime Minister. The final decision rests with the Prime
Minister, not with any one minister. This applies to finance and to any broad subject of great concern to more than one department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of Bill C-83 is to change the name of the electoral^ district of "Bonaven-ture" to that of "Bonaventure-!les-de-la-Madeleine". Doubtless, I will be allowed to make remarks somewhat more elaborate than those of the members who spoke before me because of the importance of this change to my electors of the Magdalen Islands.
It will be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that after the government of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson set up an independent commission to revise electoral boundaries, an act of parliament did away, on the electoral map, with the riding of the Magdalen Islands as a separate entity. At the same time, said act bound the territory formerly and until then occupied by the Islands to the riding of Bonaventure.
That decision of the Canadian parliament, Mr. Chairman, was very much resented by the Madelinots at the time, and I am not ready to say that the wound has healed yet. I understood, and I still do today, the normal attitude and reaction of the people of Magdalen Islands.
Indeed, I think the Magdalen Islands should get special treatment, considering their various distinguishing traits.
Firstly, they are isolated, being located and lost in the middle of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, 175 miles from Gaspe and Bonaventure and 100 miles from Prince Edward Island. Secondly, fishing is their only source of revenue. Thirdly, it is quite difficult to get to Magdalen Islands in all seasons, more so in winter when, for
February 9, 1971

instance, the hon. member for Bonaventure who lives in the western part of Bonaventure cannot easily get there on account of the precarious air and maritime transportation between Bonaventure and Magdalen Islands. Besides, air services between Gaspe or between Prince Edward Island and Magdalen Islands are extremely hazardous in winter because of frequent and severe storms. Fourthly, the insular mentality of the people of Magdalen Islands is necessarily and inevitably different.
It is easy to realize that the Iles-de-la-Madeleine must be dealt with in a special way, and we understand thus the vigourous reaction of its citizens regarding the disappearance of the riding which had been established since 1947, under the Electoral Boundaries Act.
The Iles-de-la-Madeleine have had most distinguished representatives. The first one was the father-in-law of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Gervais), the hon. Charles Cannon, Justice of the Quebec Superior Court; the second one was the ex-member for Gaspe, Mr. Russell Keays; the third one, no less distinguished, was the hon. Maurice Sauve, and since the Iles-de-la-Madeleine are linked up with Bonaventure, I have the great honour of representing the Madelinots, whom I esteem deeply.
It was specially in recognition of these characteristic features of the Madelinots and of their almost unique needs that Parliament has established, in 1947, an independent riding called "Les Iles-de-la-Madeleine".
From this time on, the Madelinots have felt more secure, having their own representative, their own member of the House of Commons, to look after them only and to deal with their problems, without having to deal with situations foreign to the Iles-de-la-Madeleine, as had been the concern of the member for Gaspe, and as it is for the member for Bonaventure.
Mr. Chairman, one must understand those feelings which are not only those of the citizens of the Iles-de-la-Madeleine but of all Canadian citizens, from Vancouver to Saint Johns, Newfoundland. So, from that time, the Madelirots were sure of having their own representative whose feelings were not divided.
That is why they reacted strongly when the riding disappeared, as they were losing, or so they thought, their real representative, their personal representative with the federal authorities. As the reason given for this change was that the population of the Islands was not large enough, it has appeared impossible, at least until now, to modify the situation and to give back a representative to the Iles-de-la-Madeleine Islands. So, this problem will be dealt with at the next census. The least that can be done for the Islands now, is to grant them some identity by adding the former name of their riding to that of Bonaventure.
The new name I am proposing is more in keeping with the geographic reality of my riding, and will enable to avoid much confusion while at the same time reflecting the pride of my Island electors who have joined my electors from Bonaventure since 1968.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT (AMENDMENT) ACT PROVISION FOR APPROVAL AND COMING INTO FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on third reading of this bill to amend the Canada-New Zealand trade agreement. The main points of the agreement are not at issue and I am sure that this bill will be passed promptly. However, I would like to say a few words about the present implication of the bill in relation to the impending trading rearrangements that must necessarily follow within a few years. These arise because of the likely entry of the United Kingdom into the European Common Market.
New Zealand, which has long valued the United Kingdom market as its main area of trade, is faced as a result of the entry into the European Common Market by Great Britain with virtual exclusion of its products from Great Britain and the common market. The British are sensitive to the needs of New Zealand and have tried to obtain from the European Common Market assurances that trade from New Zealand can enter the United Kingdom under its old preferential rate. Appreciating the value of the British market, New Zealand supported Mr. Heath at the Singapore conference to do something to counteract Soviet influence in the Indian Ocean.
Although Canada is vitally interested in the British market, especially for agricultural products, the Canadian delegation confined itself to protesting that Great Britain was not affording Canada proper recognition of the importance of Canada's exports to Great Britain, and the Prime Minister then proceeded to negate the importance of maintaining some Western influence in the Indian Ocean.
The importance of the agreement to Canada and New Zealand lies in the fact that until now New Zealand has been largely a dairy producing country depending on the British export market for butter and cheese. But with the possibility of losing drastically their trade with Great Britain in dairy products, New Zealand has introduced a change-over from dairying to beef production and has been looking for markets around the borders of the Pacific, particularly in Canada, the United States and Japan.
Trade with New Zealand was in Canada's favour until 1969, when it became roughly balanced. In 1970 until October, Canada imported $27 million worth of beef. The Canadian beef industry has always operated with a minimum of protection. The flow of beef which has been substantial shows a danger of creating dislocation in the meat industry. Since 1964 the United States has imposed quotas on beef from Australia and New Zealand. The European Common Market has imposed rigid quotas, tariffs and variable levies against all manner of agricultural products, including beef. Japan imposes a quota plus a tariff of 25 per cent of the value-cost plus freight-of beef. The United Kingdom, reversing its
New Zealand Trade Agreement Act almost century-old process of food subsidy in preference to tariff, is now in the process of instituting a system of variable levies for many agricultural products, including beef, to go into effect April 1, 1971.
It is interesting to note that in the other politically sensitive area where importation of New Zealand agricultural commodities such as butter is effectively prevented from being imported into Canada by means of an import licence, the Canadian Dairy Commission has a monopoly-85 per cent of the dairy industry is concentrated in Quebec and Ontario-and this percentage is steadily being raised by the transfer of quotas from the Prairies. This means that the dairy industry will not have to bear any competition from New Zealand, particularly in dairy sensitive areas of eastern Canada. But in the matter of beef production and other forms of meat there is really nothing in this bill that will help even at times of a very severe dislocation of our market. Last year about 7 per cent of the beef consumed in Canada came from Australia, and this year it is estimated that 12 per cent of the beef consumed in Canada could come from Australia and New Zealand.
In the few comments I have made on trade I have indicated the importance of the British market both directly to New Zealand and indirectly to Canada. We all wish, however, that the European Common Market, in the interests of world trade, will reduce the massive walls of tariffs, quotas and other restrictions that have created in the eight years of its existence a relatively inefficient agricultural industry. In conclusion, I should like to state that Bill S-4 can be said to be largely non-argumentative and is welcomed as a means of updating the trade arrangements between New Zealand and Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT (AMENDMENT) ACT PROVISION FOR APPROVAL AND COMING INTO FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words during the third reading stage of this bill. My remarks are along the lines of those of the previous speaker in trying to bring some warning to this House and to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) regarding the situation into which we are heading. I first stated my views back in 1969 when the minister returned from a trip to Asia. One of the goodies that he brought back was, as he told us, that we would have an increase in imports of beef from New Zealand. At that time I pointed out that we really did not need that much more beef from New Zealand, that we were practically self-supporting and that we had a satisfactory trade with the United States in beef. Sometimes the products were flowing from their country into ours and sometimes it was the other way around. I also told the minister that he was encouraging imports in a pretty sensitive area.
The minister, who was good enough to reply to me, set out the situation as he saw it. However, 1 am afraid that even at that time I could not bring myself to agree with him. He pointed out that what we would be bringing in would be largely what can be described as manufacturing beef. Subsequently, I corresponded with the Department

February 9, 1971
New Zealand Trade Agreement Act
of Agriculture to find out what quantities of beef were coming in, the manner in which they were coming in and the manner in which this beef was classified. Predictably, the quantities of beef coming into this country increased to the extent that the Canadian Cattlemen's Association became alarmed, and a recent issue of their magazine carries an article by Mr. Gracey expressing the alarm of the association.
Those who are acquainted with the Canadian Cattlemen's Association know that they do not usually go to the government or raise a protest. I suppose they pride themselves on being one of the last bastions of free enterprise in Canada. Their favourite saying is: We will stand on our own feet. However, they are becoming alarmed because they think their feet will be kicked out from under them. That is the situation. The minister can afford to be bland about it, but frankly I cannot afford be so indifferent to the situation.
In the matter of dairy products we realized a number of years ago that a balance would have to be maintained because of the higher cost of dairy production in Canada as compared with New Zealand which has an extremely favourable climate. We have developed with New Zealand a quota system, an agreement or an arrangement, whereby their products can come in here if they do not unduly disrupt and, indeed, destroy our own market. Yet in discussions in this House I have not been able to obtain any commitment from the government that they are prepared to take a similar attitude with regard to beef. I have raised the question in the House as well as in the committee when the bill was before it. I asked the witnesses before the committee whether the sale by New Zealand of beef in Canada could be regarded as dumping. The answer was no. That is right because the New Zealanders are not selling beef to us any cheaper than they are selling it to their own people.
I also asked the witnesses before that committee whether quotas could be established by negotiation or by agreement, that is, whether we could establish by agreement or by negotiation the quantity of beef that may be allowed into this country. Again the answer was that under this agreement we could. I am a little baffled as to why I am unable to receive a clear and coherent answer concerning the policy that will be followed on the amount of importation of beef from New Zealand in reply to the long series of questions which I put to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), as well as in answer to the question I put in the adjournment debate to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howard).
I do not know why they are reluctant to give this information or to set out the policy, unless they do not have a policy. This is wrhat really concerns me. We had such an influx of this product into Canada last year that we were exporting it to the United States to the point where the United States stopped it at the border and said they did not want any more of it. This ban continues. As a result, of course, whatever was on the high seas at that time simply came into Canada. Canada then was forced, through its representatives, I understand, to say to New Zealand that they would have to slow down.
When I asked a question regarding this matter the other night, the answer 1 received was that if this continues the government will have to take the kind of action that needs to be taken, an answer which was not too clear. I submit to the government that this is just not good enough. I think that the beef producers of this country are entitled to know government policy. They are entitled to know how much beef will be brought into this country, what the limits are and what is the competition in terms of price and volume with which they will have to contend. I think they are entitled to know this, because the people who are producing beef in this country, the farmers and the ranchers, are putting money into production. Cattle herds are increasing. Feed-lot establishments are substantial. All this is capital investment. As I pointed out the other day, we are being urged to plant more land to forage, which means increased beef production, sheep or dairy cattle. Anyone who has followed the policies of the Minister of Agriculture knows he is not encouraging anyone to go into increased dairy production.
What really concerns me is that there is not a limit of policy set out that can be understood to have this are in the business. I think we are entitled to have this limit of policy set out; I think we are entitled to know. I do not think it is good enough to sit and wait while the government decides it may be something or may not do something, to sit and wait until the United States opens its borders and then wait until it closes its borders. According to the information that has been given to me by responsible people in government, it is possible to work out a policy. As the previous speaker said-and he was dead right-New Zealand is doing what it is because it is in a tough position with dairying and sheep and it is increasing its beef production and then exporting its problems to us. I say to the government that we have enough problems of our own. Let us not expect to handle other people's as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minisier of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to intervene only briefly for the purpose of correcting some of the misinformation, or at least wrong information, that has been given respecting the magnitude of beef imports during the past few months. I am surprised that people from the great agricultural areas of Canada, particularly those areas that are dependent on export markets for most of their economy, would be advocating protectionism and restrictions in advance, because we know that these kinds of moves lead to retaliatory or what some people call compensatory action by other countries. It seems to me it is in the interests of Canada, which has a very highly efficient beef and other meat producing establishment, to do as little as possible to encourage other countries to throw up barriers against it.
To get back to the substance of the matter with respect to the statistics that have been given, some figures have been thrown around to the effect that we have been importing from 10 per cent to 12 per cent of Canada's beef requirements from oceanic countries. I do not know
[Mr. Gleave.)
February 9, 1971

where these figures came from, but they are completely erroneous. I do not have the exact figures in front of me, but speaking from memory the amount of beef imported for use in Canada during the first nine or ten months of 1970 was in the order of 60 million pounds as compared with a total production in Canada of something like 1.8 million pounds or, in effect, about 3 per cent. The fact is that there was some transshipment of beef through Canada from the latter part of 1969 until July 2, 1970, and this was destined for U.S. packing houses for use in the manufacturing industry. This was manufacturing beef. I hope hon. members will bear in mind that the greatest amount of manufacturing beef coming into Canada is frozen blocks of beef, just to fill in the deficiency in Canadian production for those purposes; and almost all of it goes into plants for processing and manufacturing.
I admit that some attempts were made to put this frozen meat on the fresh meat market, but I know of none that have been very successful because it was not comparable with the product produced here in Canada and offered in an unfrozen condition to housewives, that is, a product that has never been frozen. I hope hon. members are not suggesting that we should now build up a series of barriers to this kind of trade, which to my mind is legitimate because we do not have enough production to supply the requirements. I do not think it would be in our interests at this time, and perhaps not at any time, or at least until we see some serious deterioration in our own price structure, to put up these kinds of barriers.
In conclusion may I say that in our discussions with the Australian and New Zealand meat marketing agencies during the past summer, they fully realized it is in their interests to ship into Canada only that which can be absorbed to fill the deficiency and to do this at prices beneficial to them and to our producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the official opposition are glad to support this bill because it will do something very important, that is, help increase exports. It is important that we do everything possible at this time to increase exports of manufactured products. As hon. members know, manufactured products are labour intensive: they are our best weapon to combat the serious unemployment situation which we are facing. This country has not been doing too well in increasing exports of manufactured products during the past year. I received the latest report from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics today. During the past year our exports of manufactured products increased by only 4.2 per cent over the previous year. People may ask what is wrong with that. The answer is that it is not good enough. As the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) stated recently when answering a question put to him in the House, the number of jobs in Canada is increasing but the number of people looking for jobs is increasing faster.
Our work force is rapidly increasing. Young people are entering the labour force at a very rapid rate. We must provide jobs for them. Obviously jobs are not being provided at a fast enough rate: that is why unemployment is steadily increasing. It is obvious that unemployment cannot be cured by the public works method. When this party was in power a few years ago, we tried that. We were faced with the same situation. It did not work because it cost too many thousand dollars of public funds to create a single job. There is just so much that the exchequer of the country can afford at any time. Once the construction projects are completed, you are right back at square one: once again you have unemployment on your hands and you have to find jobs.
The only way to cure unemployment is to create jobs. By stimulating the economy it is possible for producers to sell in an atmosphere which will enable them to increase sales, production and employment. This does not cost the Canadian taxpayer one cent. It is the only-practical way of overcoming unemployment because it is on a continuing basis. That is what we are looking for. We in the official opposition are very glad to support this bill. This measure will do something that is most important for the country at the present time, namely, help increase sales of manufactured products. We say to the government: Get on with the job and use this tool to help you sell more manufactured products and thus produce more jobs for Canadian workers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, BORROWING, LIABILITY UNDER CONTRACTS OF INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was considered on second reading I noted that the Export Development Corporation and its activities represented a very important instrument in our trade policy. I think this has been borne out by the subsequent consideration of this bill. Through its programs of export credit insurance and export loans and guarantees, I think the Export Development Corporation has played and can
continue to play a very important role in promoting a healthy trade relationship and assist the economy. However, I think it must be noted once again that this instrument of policy can only be effective if in fact it is developed within the framework of an adequate trade policy.
This I pointed out during the second reading debate and I think it was underlined by some of the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howard) when he introduced the bill to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. He pointed out that discussion had taken place during the second reading debate on the problem of promoting the export of Canadian products and the fact that considerable emphasis must be placed on the sale and export of semi-finished products and raw materials rather than more highly manufactured products. The parliamentary secretary went on to point out that promotion of one kind of export in preference to another rests with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Still later he made reference to concerns that have been expressed about the degree of our trade with the United States and said that in this case also it is the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, rather than the corporation, that would make that kind of effort in dealing with these problems.
I think this underlines the point that some of us made at the time the bill was considered at second reading, namely, that this instrument of policy can operate effectively only if there is an adequate policy framework. It is perfectly obvious to all hon. members that some of the programs of this corporation have made a very important contribution to the Canadian economy. I draw attention to the value and importance of its operations to western Canada and particularly to my region in such things as grain sales. However, there is one area of the operations of this corporation which was included in the act originally passed in 1969 which I think requires further consideration. This has to do with the section of the act relating to foreign investment insurance. There are in fact amendments in the bill now before the House to some of the provisions of the original act which the government has found unworkable, and thus were unable to conclude with other countries the type of agreements and treaties that were originally hoped for when the act was first passed in 1969.
We are very concerned with the fact that Canada is becoming involved in this kind of business. I want to make it clear that we are dealing in this bill, and indeed in the act that is being amended, with the provision which encourages private investment in other countries. This has nothing to do with whether this is allowed or prohibited, but only with the point as to whether as a matter of public policy we will introduce programs that will have the effect of encouraging private Canadian concerns to develop enterprises in foreign countries through the instrument of insurance protection against what has been termed political risk. It has been suggested that this may be interpreted in some quarters as an attempt on Canada's part to enter, as it were, the twen-

February 9, 1971

tieth century scramble lor investment in countries that have not been so fortunate as Canada in terms of economic development. It has even been suggested that this could be interpreted as Canada becoming part of the new investment imperialism, a new form of colonialism that is becoming prevalent in the twentieth century.
I think we can question the propriety of this situation and ask whether this is a good approach to take to our international relationships. Is this sort of policy going to serve the long run interests of Canada? Secondly, I think we can question whether Canada can really compete in this league, given all the circumstances.
It seems to me that a second area of concern relates to what benefits accrue to Canada as a result of this action. It can be pointed out that there is provision in the act to safeguard Canada's interests and to ensure that in fact there will be benefit to Canada as a result of assisting or encouraging private investment of Canadian money in foreign countries. However, I suggest this is a subjective matter, one on which it is very difficult to make an objective judgment. I suggest conflicts will arise in assessing these projects in terms of the extent of the benefits that will accrue to Canada. It might very well be the case that some short-run benefits can be measured, but we have as well to take into account some of the long-run problems that will develop and determine whether in the long run we will see the growth of a resentment toward Canada of the sort that some countries now suffer.
The political implications involve subjective considerations that are very difficult to measure. We have Canada's experience, where our resources have been developed to a great extent by foreign financial assistance. Some people suggested that this was essential for the development of Canada, and given a particular set of circumstances this was possibly so. But the fact is that we in Canada did not do an adequate job of developing our own resources and of mobilizing their full potential. Consequently, in the absence of adequate facilities and machinery it was really a case of foreign capital moving in to fill the vacuum.
We now have the situation where while we are still concerned about imports of capital into Canada we are going to adopt as a feature of public policy a program that will encourage and assist the export of Canadian capital for purposes of private investment to develop other countries. I think the very real question that arises is whether this is the best way in which we as a nation can assist the developing nations of the world.
This investment insurance program has been referred to as a program to protect investments against losses due to political risks, such as war, revolution, confiscation or expropriation. It seems to me that some of the evidence which was revealed at the committee indicated not only difficulties which were encountered with the structure originally developed when the act was passed in 1969 but also very fundamental questions as to the advisability of this program.
Export Development Act
The officials and the parliamentary secretary, when they appeared before the committee, reported in answer to questions by members that there have been some 200 inquiries on behalf of international prospective investors and that this represents an interest in over 70 countries, 40 per cent of which were in the Caribbean and the remainder distributed over other parts of the world. By category of investment, 40 per cent was in respect of manufacturing, 17 per cent in respect of hotels, 15 per cent in respect of food or beverages, most of which is also manufacturing or processing, 10 per cent in financing and the balance of 15 to 20 per cent in a variety of mining, service industry, retail outlets, housing and warehousing.
It was also reported to the committee that bilateral negotiations have been carried on with 20 countries in an attempt to reach some sort of an agreement within the framework of existing legislation. It was indicated that difficulties had been encountered and that there were in fact fundamental objections on the part of some countries. Other countries just said: Look, we cannot deal with you because we are prohibited from signing an agreement under the laws which presently exist in our country.
It is now the intention of the government to change this act so that it will remove the requirement for a bilateral agreement authorizing the Export Development Corporation to provide investment insurance in cases where the minister is satisfied that the legislative atmosphere is such that Canadian investment will be adequately protected. It was also mentioned that the second requirement is that an investor must get a letter from the appropriate governmental authority of the host country that they do not object to this investment and, hopefully, that they approve.
Some questions were asked and some evidence was given concerning the negotiations that had been carried on with individual countries such as Spain, Nigeria and others. It was indicated that a great many difficulties were encountered. I do not intend to go into them in detail now. A further point of concern, as was indicated, is that there would be no difference in the manner in which the Export Development Corporation would deal with a foreign-controlled or owned company in Canada which desired to make further investment in a foreign company. In answer to a question asked by myself, Mr. Aitken said:
-we would not have any view with regard to the ownership of a particular Canadian company that came to us and wanted to make an investment abroad because after all you need not necessarily know who owns the company. The shares may be held abroad even though it appears to be entirely a Canadian company. However, with respect to the inquiries we have had I have here in front of me a list where we have given the investor a commitment to provide him with insurance in the event that we can have this bilateral arrangement. On looking over this list I see only one case where I know that the parent company is an American concern and there are some 20 on the list.
When I asked him if other companies which are foreign-owned or controlled were to make inquiries, his answer was, "We would treat them equally". I suggest there are policy implications that need to be considered

February 9, 1971
Export Development Act
by the government. These to some extent go beyond the considerations of the operations of the corporation itself and must be considered by the government as a matter of policy in establishing the framework for the operation of this corporation.
The parliamentary secretary, in answer to one of the questions put to him during the committee proceedings, indicated that it was the hope of the government that the new limitations being established in this bill with regard to export credit insurance, export loans and guarantees would last for three or four years before the government would again have to come to Parliament asking for an extension of the limits. At the same time, in answering a question concerning the foreign investment insurance provisions of this bill Mr. Aitken indicated that in so far as they could judge at this early stage of development they anticipated, or thought likely, that the firms which would take up this provision would use up approximately $120 million of the liability. That brings us very close to the $150 million limit proposed in this bill.
I would note in this regard that one of the clauses of the bill does call for the extension of the limit of liability that might be undertaken under the foreign investment clause, the extension being from $50 to $150 million. Thus, it would seem to me that if there is in fact the interest that has been indicated in this part of the bill, the government will have to come back to Parliament very shortly to ask for an extension, particularly if it wishes to continue with this measure.
I noticed in this regard that the parliamentary secretary indicated that the Department of Finance was only prepared to go up to $150 million. This indicates to me that the Department of Finance must have some doubt about this clause of the bill and that it has some questions in that regard and does not wish to see the limits of foreign investment insurance provisions extended too far. We will have to watch the operations of this part of the bill because in the long run there are very serious dangers contained in it for Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, BORROWING, LIABILITY UNDER CONTRACTS OF INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have a few minutes left at our disposal. I will not be selfish enough to take up all the time because I know other hon. members wish to speak and the minister is straining at the leash to respond to the very illuminating comments that have been made. There are one or two comments I should like to make very seriously at this time. I hope he will agree with me.
What is involved in this bill has a lot to do with our general trading position in the world. I think we are in a precarious position and need legislation of this kind, so I am glad to support it. We are in an extremely weak position in world markets. One reason is very simple: the prestige of this country greatly diminished after the Second World War. I think this is due to a number of reasons, some of them controversial, which I do not intend to go into in detail. Because of steps we have taken to reduce certain commitments, military and otherwise, in Europe and because during the Kennedy Round negotiations our negotiators, no doubt acting skilfully in bargaining in a hard way, obtained a number of concessions which benefited us in the short term, we lost a lot of friends. I recognize the importance of negotiation and the fact that you cannot be too honest on an international basis, but it is tremendously important to have a reservoir of good will and understanding.
Within a comparatively short time we will be faced with a difficult situation. No one can predict what will happen in Europe. The United Kingdom government is headed by a very determined man who apparently is going to get his country into the European community, Even today it is quite obvious that the international trading world will have great difficulty in salvaging the English market for New Zealand commodities and for sugar products from some of the other Commonwealth countries. Certainly there will no incentive to create circumstances which will permit Canada to benefit from this situation. England and some of the other Common Market nations may ultimately react to our benefit, but we are faced with that situation and our situation vis-avis the United States. We do not have the capacities of Japan, although I am not downgrading the Canadian position. I am sure that the minister, who has been over there recently, will bear me out. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was over there a few months ago, and so was my leader who publicly stated the things which he knew but which were reinforced by what he learned over there, things which the government should have known.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, acting as an innocent abroad, was publishing statements from time to time indicating that he was first discovering these very alarming facts. Where will this leave Canada? We will be faced with a very serious problem, and the minister knows it. I am not saying that he is not trying to do something about it-and perhaps this bill reflects it but I wonder whether it goes far enough. I would like to think that some time we will have a discussion. We have had many debates in this House. Unemployment is our No. 1 problem and we have to do what we can on this side of the House to awaken the government to these problems. But I think the minister should take the opportunity to initiate a debate. He should take a day of the government's time and initiate a debate on the situation. We do not have this kind of debate. If he does so, we will be glad to participate in it and decide, after he has spoken, whether we will continue to support him.
I was overseas recently and met a number of people in the European countries. I discussed with them the question of our trading relations. We must consider the extent to which we can make use of this bill and its ability in working with underdeveloped countries. We are starting what is known as the second decade for aid to developing nations. The fact that it is called the second decade is of some importance, because when the program was first initiated it was called the decade of aid to developing nations. However, it was discovered that ten years was not enough.
We must bear in mind that the gap between the developed and the developing nations is widening and it may

February 9, 1971

take 30 or 40 years to close it. In the meantime, time is against us. We cannot wait, because time does not wait and because a train of circumstances is set in motion which is leading us toward an unbridgeable chasm. The growth and the per capita wealth of the developed nations in comparison with that of the developing nations is tremendously serious. Now that the developing nations are able through various media to discover that there is a better way of life and a better world, these people will not sit idly by for an eternity and permit the situation to continue.

I am glad to have support for my point of view. I conclude with this comment. I shall read to the minister two or three paragraphs from a booklet of which the minister may be aware: it is called "Canada's Trade Policy in the Second Development Decade", written by Benjamin and Jean Higgins. It deals with the uses which we can make of such weapons as this bill, the Export Development Act and other measures to assist the developing nations through our trade policy. I am reading from page 65 of the booklet. These are words which the government may well bear in mind with respect to problems near at home. They read as follows:
But from what has been said already concerning unemployment, it should be clear that the most useful discovery of all would be a formula for modifying western industrial technology, applicable over a wide range of manufacturing activities, which would use less capital and more labour while raising productivity of both labour and capital. Here indeed is a challenge, and one that has yet to be accepted and translated into action in any country, whether advanced or underdeveloped. What is required is not merely laboratory research but application on a pilot-plan scale as well. And no matter how brilliant the engineers and the natural scientists engaged in such research, their efforts are unlikely to be crowned with success unless they understand clearly what it is they are seeking. After centuries of inventing labour-saving devices and of identifying the discovery of such devices with technological progress, it is not easy for western engineers and scientists- or for the engineers and scientists of LDCs whose training is essentially the same-to think in terms of new techniques that will use more labour rather than less, while raising output per man-hour and per unit of capital. But we cannot say that no such technology exists, because no one has tried seriously to find it. If Canada could produce such a technology-*
I interpolate here to say that I wish Canada could produce such a technology and export it using the medium of the Export Development Bank.
-it would be a boon to mankind.
Technical assistance programs are essentially a device whereby the existing stock of skills and the flow from the educational system are supplemented through international transfers of human resources. Very often the lack of certain types of human resources is the major bottleneck in the development of a particular country and the major factor limiting capacity to absorb capital assistance. In such cases transfers of any type of scarce skills can be helpful.
From the analysis above, however, it is clear that the most useful form of technical assistance in the Second Development Decade will be provision of those managerial, scientific, and technical skills needed to ferret out opportunities to establish successful new industrial enterprises, to organize them, and to nurse them through their infancy. In Canada these skills are
Export Development Act
usually found in private enterprises rather than in government departments or universities.
I am waiting for some approval from my friends to the left, but apparently they are not interested.
One way of making such skills available to the LDCs, obviously, is through the establishment of new Canadian enterprises in those countries. But this method may not always be appropriate, and ways must be found of making the skills of private enterprise available to our foreign-aid program. The new private enterprise division of the Canadian international development agency could prove very useful in this respect.
This may not be completely relevant, but I point out to the minister that this is a technique by which we can be of assistance to the developing countries through the effectiveness of this bill. I commend these thoughts to the minister's attention when this bill is passed and he administers it.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I have paraphrased the hon. member's words, but he implied that if we send Canadian companies to take their place in the markets of other countries we will somehow inherit the opprobrium that has fallen on a number of other nations which did this. I cannot accept that premise. I believe we have a responsibility to take our talents and invest them abroad, if this will help other nations, and I believe that the points raised by the hon. member for Peace River are worth remembering in that regard.
We have an obligation that we have accepted in international aid. We are seeking to achieve a target of 1 per cent of our gross national product as aid to the developing nations. We know that this is a difficult objective for a country the size of Canada, but the United Nations and other authorities in this field are more and more encouraging the development of foreign investment in the developing countries as a legitimate and useful way in which the developed countries can aid those nations. I believe this is useful to those nations not just because of the wealth it creates for them but because of the skills we are able to transfer to them and the managerial techniques. The plants we establish bring wealth to them as well as to Canadian corporations. In doing so, I think

February 9, 1971
Export Development Act
we must recognize that we should be prepared to abide by the laws that those nations may want to apply to Canadian corporations operating within their boundaries. We should be willing to accede to their desire that such corporations should be good corporate citizens. But that does not preclude Canadian corporations performing a very useful and valuable service to them and to us. It is for that purpose that this part of the bill has been included.
The hon. member mentioned that during committee discussions we dealt with the question of foreign-owned corporations in Canada being eligible for this benefit. Well, it is possible that this can happen, and Mr. Hugh Aiken, the chairman of the Export Development Corporation, indicated that in some cases it had happened. I make no apology for this. A corporation which operates in Canada brings wealth to Canada and should qualify for the same benefits as a Canadian citizen or Canadian corporation.
The hon. member also mentioned the $150 million limit, which he indicated would not last very long. I think this may be true. I think it is quite possible that we will reach that limit very soon, but I do not think that the reluctance of the Department of Finance or of the Treasury Board to authorize higher limits in this case was because they feared the money was not well invested. I think it was simply because there were outer limits beyond which the Canadian budget could not go at that time.
Now I wish to make some comments on the statements made by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees). He seems to have hit-and-run: I do not see him in the House at the moment.
