EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTION BY SOMALIA RESPECTING ELIMINATION OF TRADE WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, November 30, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question, as recorded on page 1584 of Hansard:
Has the government of Canada had an opportunity to evaluate the suggestion put forward by the government of Somalia to the United Nations that South Africa's major trading partners
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
hold meetings to discuss ways and means of eliminating their trade with South Africa and, if so, is the government of Canada considering initiating such consultations?
In his reply the Prime Minister indicated that the placing of an embargo on trade with South Africa had been discussed on numerous occasions at the United Nations and that the major trading nations had succeeded in defeating any such move. The clear implication of his answer is that Canada has no intention of even surveying the possibility of precipitating talks of the type which Somalia has suggested. I submit that he rejected the idea without even looking at the speech by the ambassador of Somalia in which the suggestion was made.
I was very impressed by the presentation of the ambassador of Somalia. It displayed a reasonableness and sensitivity to the problems which would confront major trading nations should an embargo on trade with South Africa be imposed, which one can hope for but which one has no right to expect from the representative of an African nation discussing apartheid. The ambassador in his speech acknowledged the dislocation which might be occasioned within the economies of South Africa's major trading partners should an embargo be imposed. He acknowledged as potentially valid the fears of South Africa's major trading partners that total compliance with such an embargo might not be achieved, with the result that some nations might make considerable sacrifices only to see other less scrupulous countries profit by seizing upon the opportunity thus provided to increase their own exports to South Africa, thereby making the sacrifice fruitless. The ambassador also acknowledged the undesirability of committing the United Nat'ons to actions which it could not follow through. The ambassador was simply asking that South Africa's major trading partners get together to seek ways and means of avoiding the problems I have outlined, in the hope that such talks might ult'mately result in making it possible for the United Nations to take effective action against South Africa's racist government.
I was simply asking the Prime Minister if his government was willing to take the initiative in this regard. His answer to me implied a total lack of interest in the proposal, and the reasons for his lack of interest are not difficult to discover. First, the government's white paper on foreign policy makes it quite obvious that for as long as this federal government remains in office, Canada's primary foreign policy objective will be to make all the money it can. Answers which I have recently received to questions I placed on the Order Paper make it plain that in South Africa Canada is making more money with a vengeance. In answer to question No. 177 on the Order Paper I was informed that Canada's exports to South Afr'ca in 1970 were expected to be approximately 30 per cent more in value than they were in 1969 and would likely exceed the 100 million mark. I realize the total value of our exports to South Africa, even at their

February 9, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion new level, represents only a small percentage of our total export trade. The point is that they are increasing at a proportionately high rate and that the increase represents a victory of the dollar over the human conscience.
If I may be permitted a brief aside at this point, I find it deplorable that this government's policies should have also resulted in a 30 per cent increase in imports of sugar from South Africa at a time when our imports of sugar from Caribbean nations, which desperately require the revenue thus to be gained, are dropping off. I submit that the unwillingness of this government actively to seek ways and means of reducing or eliminating trade with South Africa, let alone its permitting increased trade with that nation, is a cause for shame on the part of every Canadian. I submit that those who argue, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs often does, that there is nothing to be gained from isolating the South African regime-the corollary of which is that there is something to be gained through reinforcmg it through trade-are engaging in the same sort of self-deception as those who put forward similar arguments with respect to Nazi Germany in the 1930's.
The authors of the Black Paper had this to say:
-the value of Canada's economic disengagement from southern Africa should not be measured in immediate economic terms. It is important that some at least of the western nations demonstrate publicly that they are more concerned with the denial of basic human rights in southern Africa and the implications this has for human dignity everywhere than they are with short run financial benefit. A stronger Canadian policy would help to prevent the southern African confrontation from becoming an alliance of the white and wealthy west against the black majority. Already the southern African issue is causing serious rifts at the United Nations and within the Commonwealth. It is in Canada's national interest that these institutions operate successfully and expand their capabilities as multinational, multiracial forums for the resolution of international tensions.
Surely it is not too much to ask that our government take the extremely timid step of beginning the discussions suggested by Somalia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Miichell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTION BY SOMALIA RESPECTING ELIMINATION OF TRADE WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the question asked by the hon. gentleman I looked up the proceedings of the United Nations General Assembly to see the origin of the proposal that had been made by the ambassador of Somalia. None of the resolutions ultimately passed by the General Assembly contained, to our knowledge, the suggestion made by the ambassador of Somalia. I would have to get confirmation from our permanent mission in New York, but it would appear that there has been no follow-up whatever to the suggestion and no consultations have been initiated by anyone.
I might add, however, that we have carefully considered the general question of cutting off trade with South Africa. In the foreign policy papers which were published last year we discussed the issues that are involved. I would point out to the hon. member that the principle that Canada has adhered to for a long time, with the exception of sanctions which have been approved by the United Nations, is one of not refusing to trade with a

nation because we disapprove of its form of government or find its action to be repugnant. X can assure the hon. member that the actions of the South African government in enforcing apartheid are as repugnant to us as they are to him.
We have been urged on many occasions to break off trading with countries because people do not agree with the policies followed by those countries. I would remind my hon. friend that we have been urged to break trading relations with Cuba and with Communist China. We have refused to do so. We believe that we should encourage trade as a means of making useful contacts between peoples. We believe that this is a principle that is worth preserving and that we should follow our practice, as in the past, of breaking trading relations only when sanctions are approved by the United Nations.

subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-REGINA-MEETINGS WITH CITY REGARDING SALE OF CITY-OWNED PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time negotiations have been carried on between the city of Regina and the Department of Transport concerning the transfer of operations of the Regina municipal airport to the Department of Transport. One of the factors involved in making this transfer is an acreage of land that is still owned by the city of Regina but which was an integral part of the airport property. On January 15 I addressed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), as reported at page 2445 of Hansard as follows:
Will the minister be holding further meetings with the city of Regina with regard to the sale of city-owned property at the Regina airport? If so, will the minister inform the House when such meetings will be held?
The Minister of Transport replied that arrangements had just been made for a further meeting with the mayor and other officials of the city of Regina. Subsequently on January 29 I addressed another question to the Minister of Transport, reported at page 2894 as follows:
Can the minister indicate whether any progress was made at the meetings this week with the city of Regina concerning the proposed sale of land by the city to the federal Department of Transport at the Regina airport, and can he give any indication when we may expect to have an agreement signed on this matter and also dealing with the future operation of Regina airport?
The Minister of Transport answered:
Considerable progress was made at the meetings this week with the mayor of Regina and other officials of that city. As I recall the timetable, we are going to Regina practically at the same time as the meetings will be held in Saskatoon to which I referred a few minutes ago, and I would hope that if we do not resolve the matter completely at that time it will be sufficiently advanced so that the contracts can be signed and the whole deal completed within the present year.
I am very happy to see that progress has been made in resolving the problem at Regina airport. The purpose of my intervention is not to be at all abrasive in respect of
February 9, 1971

negotiations which are now going on. I welcome the tact that progress has been made and I note that negotiations are to continue. I hope they will be successful. I urge the government to do everything in its power to ensure that a satisfactory agreement is reached.
In this respect I want to outline a few matters which have been of concern to the people of Regina and area regarding this matter. I am going to deal with this in a somewhat disjointed fashion since a notice of motion for the production of papers which I placed on the Order Paper on December 15 has not yet been called by the government. That notice of motion asked for a copy of all correspondence and other documents concerning the proposed sale of land owned by the city of Regina at the Regina airport to the Department of Transport.
Some of the points concerned were dealt with in an article in the Regina Leader Post of December 11 last. I might say that this was prior to the recent meetings which were held. The article stated in part:
Negotiations over the proposed sale of airport land in Regina to the federal government have been stalled, with the government refusing to accept the value placed on the land by two Independent appraisers-
It was also noted as follows:
Involved are 320 acres of airport land which the federal Department of Transport requires if it is to assume operation of the airport as it announced in 1967.
In reports prepared this summer, the two appraisers, Warren-Hawes Real Estate and Vernon Peterson of the provincial highways department, had assessed the land value at $16,285 and $15,400 an acre respectively-
Later on in the article it is pointed out that there are other contentions made by the city which will presently be negotiated regarding the computed value of the rent of the land which is owned by the city and being used at the Regina airport operations since January, 1968, when the last agreement between the city and the Department of Transport expired. There was a statement made by the mayor of Regina, in December last, when he referred to one point upon which I should like to hear the comments of the parliamentary secretary. This was his statement:
Since then the Minister of Transport and his department officials have consistently refused to accept the agreed appraisals and present them to the Treasury Board with recommendation for payment according to the agreement with the city

Later on it was stated that last March the transport minister agreed that the price of the land would be established by two separate qualified appraisers. I hope the parliamentary secretary can throw some light on these matters and that progress will be made in negotiations. My purpose in drawing this to the attention of the government tonight is to urge the government to do everything to ensure that a satisfactory agreement is reached.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED OIL PIPELINE FROM PRUDHOE BAY TO VALDEZ, ALASKA-CONSULTATION WITH UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say at the outset how pleased I am to see the minister here during this adjournment debate. I presume he is here to respond to the question raised. Too often those of us who participate in these debates on a fairly regular basis receive a 3-minute reply prepared by someone in advance a reply which has nothing at all to do with the particular representation we make. So I welcome the minister here and look forward to his response.
In recent weeks various Members of Parliament have raised the question of the threat to Canada's west coast ecology by the transshipment of Prudhoe Bay oil, first by pipeline to Valdez Island, Alaska and then by tanker to Cherry Point in Puget Sound which is just a few miles from the Canadian border. Members from Esquimalt-Saanich, Edmonton East, Kootenay West and I have all been attempting, possibly fruitlessly, to spur the Department of External Affairs into action, but as yet-in spite of our representations-we received nothing in reassurance from the minister.
It seems that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has been unduly reticent about this extremely serious matter. I realize that it is fraught with difficulties for him. Tankers are currently being built by

February 9, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the Bethlehem Steel Company in the United States which, according to my information, have a capacity of about 100,000 tons, and these are reputed to be planned to ply off our west coast for periods of up to 20 years. These 100,000-ton monsters are giants compared to the 18,000-ton Arrow which ran aground in Chedabucto Bay last year. At that time, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) suffered at least a week of sleepless nights over this threat, and what could he expect if one of these 100,000-ton monsters went aground? I do not think the Minister of Transport can last as long as a month without sleep.
These 100,000-ton tankers in trouble can cause approximately six times the amount of damage that was caused by the Arrow grounding. In addition, this is a very sensitive area in Canada. The Boundary Bay, Puget Sound area is very close to our area and Puget Sound is the only marine productive area in Canada. Anyone familiar with marine productivity of tidal flats cannot fail to be alarmed at what a tanker wreck could do to Canada's south western ecology. I think it can be accepted that fishing could be ruined in large parts of our spawning areas for years to come and water fowl, resting and recreation areas such as beaches would also run the risk of being defiled for years ahead.
During the debate of the bill of the Minister of Transport to amend the Canada Shipping Act last October, a bill which was designed precisely to protect our shores from the kind of tanker pollution of which we are now fearful, my party strongly urged the minister to extend Canada's sovereignty in regard to pollution at least 100 miles off shore instead of the measly 12 miles proposed in the bill. Other countries have done this. The United States has gone out to its tidal shelf for a number of reasons into which I have not time to go now. Peru has done so; and even we saw fit to extend our sovereignty 100 miles out in the Arctic. If this had been done last October when we were debating the bill, if the minister had accepted the suggestion warmly, I think it would have served as a warning to the Americans that we will not tolerate the possible devastation of the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
In that case perhaps the oil companies concerned, who have obviously committed to this plan if oil tankers are under construction, might have been impressed with the need to locate their refinery further south instead of just on our border, perhaps in southern Washington, Oregon or California. However, this did not happen and we have been left with Hobson's choice: either Canada accepts tanker oil off our west coast or we may be moved to rationalize future Alaskan oil movement through the corridor which is now being proposed to carry natural gas. Either choice is agonizing. Simply put, the case is whether Canada is prepared to risk its marine or Arctic ecology. It is a horrid position in which to be put.
It is fair to say that U.S. energy demands are only beginning to be felt, and it behoves Canada to depart from its historic timid, perhaps deferential position of
reacting to U.S. initiative, and instead began to assert its own initiative in this U.S. energy game. The United States are desperately short of energy because of their population growth and because they squandered their own resources during the last 200 years. Therefore, I submit that we are in a very strong bargaining position and we will be more respected if we begin to assert ourselves. One of the things that might be agreed upon is an Arctic corridor.
I am sure the minister is anxious to respond, Mr. Speaker, because I know he is concerned about the question. Perhaps he feels it is beyond his jurisdiction, but I would like to hear him agree with our concern and say that he has made preparation to discuss this matter seriously with Washington and offer alternatives.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED OIL PIPELINE FROM PRUDHOE BAY TO VALDEZ, ALASKA-CONSULTATION WITH UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government shares the concern of the hon. member regarding possible damage to the coasts of Canada and the United States which could result from the massive movement of oil by tanker from Valdez to the United States Pacific northwest. We intend to discuss the hazards involved with the United States authorities at an appropriate time.
Oil spills would affect the United States as well as the Canadian coastline. This is a concern that we have in common. It really does not matter on the Pacific coast where a spill occurs, because some of it will affect both countries. In view of the interest which the United States shares with Canada in protecting the environment, it would be my hope that both countries will take such action as lies within their respective jurisdictions to ensure that the movement of oil does not despoil the Pacific coastline of our two countries.
So long as tankers confine themselves to the U.S. side of the boundary line, they will be wholly within United States waters. Canada, of course, cannot legislate concerning traffic on that side of the border. I say to the hon. member that even the declaration of a 100-mile or 200-mile limit would not affect the position in the Straits of Juan de Fuca. This is very much a problem that concerns our two countries and cannot be resolved by unilateral action on our part.

speechtext: What about farther north?

But that is not where the problem is going to arise. They are going to regularize this traffic through the Straits of Juan de Fuca.
However, it is the view of the Canadian government that a country is obliged to prevent activities within its jurisdiction from damaging persons or property within the territory of any other country through pollution of the environment. It might be of some value to request the International Joint Commission to study the risks of pollution which might result from heavy tanker traffic through the Juan de Fuca Strait. As the hon. member knows, the United States government is still studying environmental considerations relating to the construction of a pipeline across Alaska. We are following this matter very closely. However, I do not think it would be appro-
